nodes.name: Medieval music
nodes.description: Western sacred and secular music of the medieval era: chant, troubadour song, and early polyphony. Dates delimit a historical era, not the end of its living repertoire.

nodes.name: Renaissance music
nodes.description: Interwoven vocal polyphony, masses, motets, and madrigals in Renaissance Europe. Era boundaries are approximate; the repertoire is still performed.

nodes.name: Baroque music
nodes.description: Basso continuo, opera, concertos, and contrapuntal invention. Approximate dates mark the historical era, not the disappearance of Baroque performance.

nodes.name: Classical era
nodes.description: The Classical period, not the umbrella term classical music: balanced phrases, sonata form, symphonies, and string quartets. Its historical boundaries overlap the Romantic era.

nodes.name: Romantic music
nodes.description: Expanded orchestras, expressive harmony, virtuoso soloists, and musical storytelling. Dates describe a historical era whose repertoire remains active.

nodes.name: Modern classical
nodes.description: An umbrella for modern and contemporary Western art music, from impressionism and modernism to experimental composition. Not a single unified style.

nodes.name: Minimalism
nodes.description: Repetition, sustained tones, gradual processes, and shifting patterns in experimental composition. One strand of modern classical music, with a reach into rock and electronic music.

nodes.name: Blues
nodes.description: African American musical traditions shaped by expressive vocal phrasing, blue notes, and recurring harmonic forms. A major source for jazz, rhythm and blues, and rock and roll.

nodes.name: Jazz
nodes.description: African American music emerging in New Orleans around the turn of the twentieth century, built on improvisation, rhythmic interplay, and blues traditions. The umbrella for many distinct jazz styles.

nodes.name: Swing
nodes.description: Dance-oriented jazz with buoyant rhythmic swing and arranged big-band sections, central to the 1930s and 1940s and still played today.

nodes.name: Bebop
nodes.description: Small-group jazz with fast tempos, intricate melodies, and improvisation over rapidly moving chord changes. A foundational language of modern jazz.

nodes.name: Cool jazz
nodes.description: Restrained dynamics, lighter timbres, and carefully arranged textures in postwar jazz. Includes, but is not synonymous with, West Coast jazz.

nodes.name: Hard bop
nodes.description: Bebop extended through blues, gospel, and rhythm-and-blues phrasing, with a strong groove and earthy ensemble sound.

nodes.name: Modal jazz
nodes.description: Improvisation organized around modes and longer harmonic spaces rather than dense sequences of chord changes.

nodes.name: Free jazz
nodes.description: Jazz that experiments with or abandons fixed chord progressions, regular meter, and conventional ensemble roles in favor of freer improvisation.

nodes.name: Jazz fusion
nodes.description: Jazz improvisation meets rock amplification, electric instruments, and funk rhythms. An evolving family of approaches rather than a single formula.

nodes.name: Rock and roll
nodes.description: A mid-century synthesis of rhythm and blues, country, gospel, and boogie-woogie, driven by a strong backbeat. The launching point for later rock styles.

nodes.name: Rock
nodes.description: The broad guitar-centered family that developed from rock and roll, encompassing many approaches to songwriting, amplification, and band performance.

nodes.name: Blues rock
nodes.description: Electric blues vocabulary played with rock volume and rhythm, often emphasizing guitar solos and extended improvisation.

nodes.name: Psychedelic rock
nodes.description: Rock expanded through studio experimentation, unusual timbres, long improvisations, and the counterculture of the 1960s.

nodes.name: Progressive rock
nodes.description: Rock explored through extended forms, shifting meters, concept albums, and elements of classical music and jazz.

nodes.name: Hard rock
nodes.description: Heavy guitar riffs, forceful drums, and powerful vocals grew out of blues and garage rock into a durable arena and club sound.

nodes.name: Heavy metal
nodes.description: Amplified heaviness, distortion, emphatic riffs, and dramatic performance developed from late-1960s hard rock.

nodes.name: Punk rock
nodes.description: Short, urgent songs and a do-it-yourself ethos challenged rock spectacle and helped establish independent musical networks.

nodes.name: Post-punk
nodes.description: Punk's independence redirected into experimental structures, angular guitars, and influences from dub, funk, and electronic music.

nodes.name: Alternative rock
nodes.description: An umbrella for rock developing outside the mainstream through independent labels, college radio, and underground scenes before its 1990s breakthrough.

nodes.name: Grunge
nodes.description: A Pacific Northwest alternative-rock scene combining punk abrasion and metal weight, brought to international attention in the early 1990s.

nodes.name: Hildegard of Bingen
nodes.description: Medieval composer of sacred monophonic songs and the music drama Ordo Virtutum. Dates approximate her documented composing period, not her lifespan.

nodes.name: Léonin
nodes.description: Notre-Dame school composer associated with early polyphonic organum. Activity dates are approximate because biographical evidence is limited.

nodes.name: Pérotin
nodes.description: Notre-Dame school composer known for large-scale polyphonic organum. Dates indicate an approximate period of activity.

nodes.name: Josquin des Prez
nodes.description: Renaissance composer of masses, motets, and secular vocal works.

nodes.name: Giovanni Pierluigi da Palestrina
nodes.description: Italian Renaissance composer celebrated for sacred vocal polyphony.

nodes.name: William Byrd
nodes.description: English composer of sacred polyphony, consort music, and keyboard works.

nodes.name: Johann Sebastian Bach
nodes.description: German Baroque composer whose sacred, orchestral, and keyboard works unite intricate counterpoint with expressive harmony.

nodes.name: George Frideric Handel
nodes.description: Baroque composer of operas, oratorios, and instrumental music, with a career centered in London.

nodes.name: Antonio Vivaldi
nodes.description: Venetian Baroque composer and violinist, especially associated with the solo concerto.

nodes.name: Joseph Haydn
nodes.description: Classical composer central to the development of the symphony and string quartet.

nodes.name: Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart
nodes.description: Classical composer of operas, concertos, symphonies, and chamber music, active from childhood.

nodes.name: Ludwig van Beethoven
nodes.description: Composer whose symphonies, sonatas, and quartets bridge Classical forms and Romantic expression.

nodes.name: Frédéric Chopin
nodes.description: Romantic composer and pianist who transformed the expressive language of solo piano music.

nodes.name: Pyotr Ilyich Tchaikovsky
nodes.description: Romantic composer of symphonies, operas, concertos, and ballet scores.

nodes.name: Claude Debussy
nodes.description: French composer whose colors and harmonic innovations helped reshape music at the turn of the twentieth century.

nodes.name: Arnold Schoenberg
nodes.description: Modernist composer associated with atonality and the development of twelve-tone composition.

nodes.name: Igor Stravinsky
nodes.description: Composer whose career spans Russian ballets, neoclassicism, and serial works. The end marks his last completed compositions.

nodes.name: Steve Reich
nodes.description: American composer known for phasing, repeating patterns, and gradual musical processes.

nodes.name: Philip Glass
nodes.description: American composer whose repetitive structures extend across ensemble works, operas, and film scores.

nodes.name: Terry Riley
nodes.description: American composer whose In C helped establish a flexible, repeating-pattern approach to minimalism.

nodes.name: Robert Johnson
nodes.description: Delta blues singer and guitarist whose small recorded catalogue became influential in later blues and rock.

nodes.name: Muddy Waters
nodes.description: Singer and guitarist central to the amplified Chicago blues sound.

nodes.name: B.B. King
nodes.description: Blues singer and guitarist celebrated for lyrical phrasing and an expressive single-note guitar style.

nodes.name: Louis Armstrong
nodes.description: New Orleans trumpeter and singer whose improvisation helped make the jazz soloist central to the music.

nodes.name: Duke Ellington
nodes.description: Pianist, bandleader, and composer whose orchestra expanded jazz's expressive and structural possibilities.

nodes.name: Jelly Roll Morton
nodes.description: New Orleans pianist, bandleader, and composer associated with early jazz arrangements.

nodes.name: Count Basie
nodes.description: Pianist and bandleader whose Kansas City swing emphasized blues phrasing and rhythmic economy.

nodes.name: Benny Goodman
nodes.description: Clarinetist and bandleader prominent in the swing era.

nodes.name: Charlie Parker
nodes.description: Alto saxophonist whose melodic and harmonic innovations were central to bebop.

nodes.name: Dizzy Gillespie
nodes.description: Trumpeter and composer central to bebop and the development of Afro-Cuban jazz.

nodes.name: Thelonious Monk
nodes.description: Pianist and composer with a distinctive rhythmic and harmonic language, associated with the emergence of bebop.

nodes.name: Miles Davis
nodes.description: Trumpeter and bandleader whose changing ensembles helped shape cool jazz, modal jazz, and electric fusion.

nodes.name: Dave Brubeck
nodes.description: Pianist and composer associated with cool jazz and experiments in unusual meters.

nodes.name: Chet Baker
nodes.description: Trumpeter and singer known for the lyrical, restrained sound of West Coast cool jazz.

nodes.name: Art Blakey
nodes.description: Drummer whose Jazz Messengers became a defining hard-bop ensemble and a training ground for younger musicians.

nodes.name: Horace Silver
nodes.description: Pianist and composer who brought blues and gospel inflections to hard bop.

nodes.name: Clifford Brown
nodes.description: Trumpeter whose work with Max Roach is a landmark of early hard bop.

nodes.name: John Coltrane
nodes.description: Saxophonist whose work moved from bebop and hard bop into modal and freer improvisation.

nodes.name: McCoy Tyner
nodes.description: Pianist associated with John Coltrane's quartet and a powerful modal harmonic language.

nodes.name: Ornette Coleman
nodes.description: Saxophonist and composer whose late-1950s ensembles helped establish free jazz.

nodes.name: Cecil Taylor
nodes.description: Pianist and composer known for percussive intensity and freely structured improvisation.

nodes.name: Albert Ayler
nodes.description: Saxophonist whose forceful, spiritually charged playing became central to 1960s free jazz.

nodes.name: Weather Report
nodes.description: Electric jazz-fusion group founded by Joe Zawinul and Wayne Shorter.

nodes.name: Mahavishnu Orchestra
nodes.description: John McLaughlin's fusion ensemble combined jazz improvisation, rock intensity, and complex rhythmic structures; activity included multiple lineups and breaks.

nodes.name: Chuck Berry
nodes.description: Guitarist and songwriter whose riffs and storytelling helped define rock and roll.

nodes.name: Little Richard
nodes.description: Singer and pianist whose explosive voice and driving rhythm became foundational to rock and roll.

nodes.name: Elvis Presley
nodes.description: Singer whose early recordings brought country and rhythm-and-blues influences to a mass rock-and-roll audience.

nodes.name: The Beatles
nodes.description: Liverpool band whose songwriting and studio experiments reshaped rock and pop.

nodes.name: The Rolling Stones
nodes.description: British band that developed a blues-based sound into one of rock's longest-running careers.

nodes.name: The Who
nodes.description: British rock band known for forceful live performance, ambitious songwriting, and rock operas.

nodes.name: Cream
nodes.description: British power trio central to blues rock. Original activity ran 1966-1968, with reunion performances in 1993 and 2005; the career envelope includes those breaks.

nodes.name: Jimi Hendrix
nodes.description: Guitarist and songwriter who expanded amplified blues and psychedelic rock through feedback, effects, and improvisation.

nodes.name: Grateful Dead
nodes.description: San Francisco band associated with psychedelic rock and long-form concert improvisation.

nodes.name: Jefferson Airplane
nodes.description: San Francisco psychedelic-rock band. Original activity ran 1965-1972, with a 1989 reunion and a final 1996 appearance; dates include those breaks.

nodes.name: Yes
nodes.description: Progressive-rock group known for extended compositions, virtuoso playing, and changing lineups.

nodes.name: King Crimson
nodes.description: Progressive-rock band with an evolving combination of complex meters, improvisation, and experimental textures. Career dates include extended breaks.

nodes.name: Genesis
nodes.description: British band that developed from theatrical progressive rock into a broader pop-rock sound, with multiple hiatuses and reunions.

nodes.name: Led Zeppelin
nodes.description: British band whose blues-based riffs helped define hard rock. Original activity ended in 1980; dates include later one-off reunions, most recently in 2007.

nodes.name: Deep Purple
nodes.description: British hard-rock band known for heavy riffs and classically inflected keyboards; its history includes a 1976-1984 breakup.

nodes.name: AC/DC
nodes.description: Australian band built on blues-derived riffs and a direct, driving hard-rock sound.

nodes.name: Black Sabbath
nodes.description: Birmingham band whose dark, heavy riffs helped establish heavy metal. Dates include breaks and the final 2025 reunion performance.

nodes.name: Judas Priest
nodes.description: British heavy-metal band known for twin-guitar arrangements and powerful vocals.

nodes.name: Iron Maiden
nodes.description: British heavy-metal band associated with galloping rhythms, harmonized guitars, and long-form storytelling.

nodes.name: Ramones
nodes.description: New York band whose fast, concise songs became a blueprint for punk rock.

nodes.name: Sex Pistols
nodes.description: British punk band whose original 1975-1978 run became culturally defining. The career envelope includes sporadic reunions and a later lineup.

nodes.name: The Clash
nodes.description: British punk band that incorporated reggae, dub, rockabilly, and other musical forms.

nodes.name: Joy Division
nodes.description: Manchester post-punk band known for stark arrangements and a brooding atmosphere.

nodes.name: Talking Heads
nodes.description: New York band combining art-school experimentation, punk-era independence, and funk-influenced rhythm.

nodes.name: The Cure
nodes.description: British band emerging from post-punk, with a catalogue ranging from stark gothic textures to pop.

nodes.name: R.E.M.
nodes.description: Athens, Georgia band whose independent-label beginnings and college-radio following helped define alternative rock.

nodes.name: Sonic Youth
nodes.description: New York band bringing alternate tunings, noise, and experimental guitar textures into alternative rock.

nodes.name: Pixies
nodes.description: American alternative-rock band known for sharp loud-quiet contrasts. Dates include a 1993-2004 breakup.

nodes.name: Nirvana
nodes.description: Washington band whose Nevermind brought grunge and alternative rock to a mass audience.

nodes.name: Pearl Jam
nodes.description: Seattle rock band associated with the early-1990s grunge breakthrough.

nodes.name: Soundgarden
nodes.description: Seattle band combining heavy riffs and unusual meters. Dates include the 1997-2010 breakup, the 2017 dissolution, and occasional reunion performances through September 2026; they do not imply continuous activity.

nodes.name: Soul
nodes.phaseNote: Illustrative editorial shading, approximately dated: classic soul peaks in the mid-1960s, then keeps a steady presence, with a lift during the late-1990s neo-soul wave. Not a measured global popularity ranking.
nodes.description: Gospel fervor meets rhythm and blues. The emotional and vocal foundation that funk, disco, and house all draw from.

nodes.name: Funk
nodes.phaseNote: Illustrative editorial shading, approximately dated: 1970s peak, then a continuing scene and sample source, with a mid-2010s pop-funk moment. Not a measured global popularity ranking.
nodes.description: Rhythm promoted to lead instrument: syncopated basslines and the one. James Brown's blueprint runs underneath electro, techno, and house.

nodes.name: Disco
nodes.phaseNote: Illustrative editorial shading, approximately dated: the late-1970s boom and backlash, then repeated comebacks — the early-2000s French touch and nu-disco wave, the 2013 retro-disco moment, and the 2020 disco-pop revival. Not a measured global popularity ranking.
nodes.description: Four-on-the-floor dance music born in New York's Black, Latino, and gay clubs. Its DJ culture and 12-inch single are the operating system of all later dance music.

nodes.name: Hip-hop
nodes.description: Bronx block-party culture built on breakbeats and turntables. Its electro branch loops straight into Detroit.

nodes.name: Krautrock
nodes.phaseNote: Illustrative editorial shading, approximately dated: the original German movement, then rediscoveries through 1990s post-rock and late-2000s reissues and neo-kraut bands. Golden age means creative peak within this scene, not mainstream dominance.
nodes.description: West German experimental rock — motorik repetition and early synthesizers. The laboratory Kraftwerk emerged from.

nodes.name: Synth-pop
nodes.description: Pop songs built entirely from synthesizers, normalized by Kraftwerk and British new wave. Beloved on Detroit radio in the early 80s.

nodes.name: Italo disco
nodes.phaseNote: Illustrative editorial shading, approximately dated: 1980s commercial peak, then a 2000s revival through electroclash and new Italo-inspired labels. Not a measured global popularity ranking.
nodes.description: Disco rebuilt in Italy with drum machines and arpeggiated synths after the US backlash. Heavily imported by Chicago and Detroit DJs.

nodes.name: Hi-NRG
nodes.phaseNote: Illustrative editorial shading, approximately dated: original club and commercial peak, followed by continuing specialist scenes. Related styles have their own histories.
nodes.description: Fast, sequencer-driven post-disco descended from Moroder's productions. Proof that machines alone could carry a dancefloor.

nodes.name: Electro
nodes.description: Hip-hop's robotic cousin: TR-808 patterns and vocoders, crystallized by 'Planet Rock'. Cybotron made it Detroit's native language.

nodes.name: Chicago house
nodes.description: Disco stripped to the drum machine and rebuilt in Chicago clubs — named after the Warehouse. The first genre authored by DJs for DJs.

nodes.name: Garage house
nodes.description: The soulful, gospel-leaning New York strain of house, named after Larry Levan's Paradise Garage.

nodes.name: Deep house
nodes.description: House slowed and softened with jazz chords and soul vocals, defined by Larry Heard's 'Can You Feel It'.

nodes.name: Acid house
nodes.description: The squelch of a misused Roland TB-303, discovered by Phuture. Detonated UK youth culture in 1988.

nodes.name: Detroit techno
nodes.description: The Belleville Three fused funk, electro, and European synth music into futurist machine soul. Named by Juan Atkins; the trunk of the entire techno tree.

nodes.name: Minimal techno
nodes.description: Techno reduced to its skeleton — one idea, slowly mutated. Pioneered by Robert Hood and Richie Hawtin out of Detroit's second wave.

nodes.name: Dub techno
nodes.description: Berlin's Basic Channel ran Detroit techno through dub reggae's echo chambers: chords dissolved into fog.

nodes.name: Trance
nodes.description: German strain of techno and acid house stretched into long hypnotic builds, born around Frankfurt.

nodes.name: Gabber
nodes.description: Rotterdam's answer to Detroit: techno pushed past 160 BPM with distorted kicks.

nodes.name: Breakbeat hardcore
nodes.phaseNote: Illustrative editorial shading, approximately dated: original UK rave peak, then a specialist scene and a 2010s rave-revival comeback. Not an extinction date.
nodes.description: UK rave's first mutation: acid house energy welded to sped-up hip-hop breakbeats. The big bang of the UK continuum.

nodes.name: Jungle
nodes.phaseNote: Illustrative editorial shading, approximately dated: original 1990s UK breakthrough, a long underground stretch, then a clear late-2010s revival. Not a measured global popularity ranking.
nodes.description: Hardcore's breakbeats chopped into polyrhythms over reggae basslines — Black British sound-system culture at rave tempo.

nodes.name: Drum and bass
nodes.description: Jungle refined into a sleeker, technoid form — rolling breaks at 170+ BPM.

nodes.name: UK garage
nodes.phaseNote: Illustrative editorial shading, approximately dated: late-1990s UK commercial peak, a quieter stretch, then a gradual 2010s–2020s revival. Not a measured global popularity ranking.
nodes.description: US garage house pitched up and swung for London, absorbing jungle's bass culture into 2-step.

nodes.name: Dubstep
nodes.description: UK garage hollowed out in Croydon: half-tempo sway, sub-bass pressure, dub space.

nodes.name: Kraftwerk
nodes.description: Düsseldorf's man-machines. 'Trans-Europe Express' and 'Computer World' are cited by Juan Atkins and Afrika Bambaataa alike as the source code.
nodes.phaseNote: Editorial career prominence anchored to Autobahn, Trans-Europe Express, Computer World, and the 2003 Tour de France Soundtracks return. This describes recording-era visibility, not the continuing magnitude of Kraftwerk's influence or measured listening.

nodes.name: Giorgio Moroder
nodes.description: Munich producer whose fully sequenced 'I Feel Love' (1977) proved electronic dance music could be the future, not a gimmick.

nodes.name: Juan Atkins
nodes.description: The originator: coined 'techno', recorded as Cybotron and Model 500, founded Metroplex. One third of the Belleville Three.

nodes.name: Derrick May
nodes.description: The innovator of the Belleville Three. 'Strings of Life' gave techno its emotional ceiling; founded Transmat.

nodes.name: Kevin Saunderson
nodes.description: The elevator of the Belleville Three. Took techno to the pop charts with Inner City; founded KMS.

nodes.name: Belleville Three
nodes.description: Atkins, May, and Saunderson — high-school friends from Belleville, Michigan, who invented Detroit techno between mixtapes and Metroplex.

nodes.name: Cybotron
nodes.description: Juan Atkins and Rik Davis. 'Clear' (1983) is the hinge between electro and techno.

nodes.name: Frankie Knuckles
nodes.description: The Godfather of House. His edits and drum-machine experiments as Warehouse resident birthed the genre that took the club's name.

nodes.name: Ron Hardy
nodes.description: Music Box resident whose raw, manic sets made Chicago's wildest records — he broke 'Acid Tracks' from a cassette.

nodes.name: Larry Levan
nodes.description: Paradise Garage resident; his eclectic, emotional marathon sets defined garage house and modern DJ culture.

nodes.name: Phuture
nodes.description: DJ Pierre, Spanky, and Herb J. Twisting a TB-303's knobs past reason, they invented acid house with 'Acid Tracks'.

nodes.name: Jeff Mills
nodes.description: The Wizard. Co-founded Underground Resistance, then defined hard minimal techno on Axis and early Tresor.

nodes.name: Underground Resistance
nodes.description: Detroit's masked, militant second-wave collective — techno as Black liberation politics, no major labels, no faces.

nodes.name: Richie Hawtin
nodes.description: Windsor's Plastikman, across the river from Detroit. Stripped acid and techno down to minimal's blueprint.

nodes.name: Carl Craig
nodes.description: Second-wave Detroit polymath, May's protégé — stretched techno toward jazz and orchestras on Planet E.

nodes.name: Goldie
nodes.description: Graffiti writer turned jungle auteur. 'Timeless' and his Metalheadz label took drum and bass to the world.
nodes.phaseNote: Editorial career prominence centered on the early jungle singles and the 1995 Timeless breakthrough, followed by ongoing production and later releases. This is scene-relative editorial shading, not a ranking against mainstream artists or measured listening.

nodes.name: Metroplex
nodes.description: Juan Atkins' label — release M-001, Model 500's 'No UFO's', is techno's founding document.

nodes.name: Transmat
nodes.description: Derrick May's label. 'Strings of Life' and the Transmat seal: emotional futurism from Detroit.

nodes.name: KMS
nodes.description: Kevin Saunderson's label, bridge between Detroit techno and the global charts via Inner City.

nodes.name: Trax Records
nodes.description: Chicago's chaotic house factory — 'Acid Tracks', 'Your Love', and most of the genre's canon on recycled vinyl.

nodes.name: Tresor
nodes.description: Berlin club and label in a bank vault under Potsdamer Platz; the Detroit–Berlin axis made concrete after the Wall fell.

nodes.name: Detroit
nodes.description: Post-industrial Motor City. Assembly lines, WGPR radio, and The Electrifying Mojo set the conditions for techno.

nodes.name: Chicago
nodes.description: Where disco survived its backlash underground and mutated into house.

nodes.name: New York
nodes.description: Birthplace of disco DJ culture, hip-hop, and the Paradise Garage.

nodes.name: Düsseldorf
nodes.description: Rhineland industrial city; home of Kraftwerk's Kling Klang studio.

nodes.name: Berlin
nodes.description: Reunified city of empty vaults and power plants that adopted Detroit techno as its soundtrack.

nodes.name: London
nodes.description: Sound-system capital where acid house became rave, and rave became a 30-year continuum.

nodes.name: I Feel Love
nodes.description: Donna Summer, produced by Giorgio Moroder — the first all-sequencer dance hit. Eno: 'This is the sound of the future.'

nodes.name: Clear
nodes.description: Cybotron's electro landmark: the exact midpoint between 'Planet Rock' and techno.

nodes.name: No UFO's
nodes.description: Model 500 (Juan Atkins), Metroplex M-001. Widely cited as the first techno record.

nodes.name: Strings of Life
nodes.description: Rhythim Is Rhythim (Derrick May). Piano stabs and strings with no bassline — techno's emotional anthem.

nodes.name: Acid Tracks
nodes.description: Phuture on Trax. Twelve minutes of TB-303 squelch that named and defined acid house.

nodes.name: Your Love
nodes.description: Frankie Knuckles and Jamie Principle — Chicago house's tenderest anthem.

nodes.name: The Warehouse
nodes.description: Frankie Knuckles' Chicago club. Members-only, mostly Black and gay — 'house music' is literally its record-store shorthand.

nodes.name: Paradise Garage
nodes.description: Larry Levan's New York church of sound; 'garage' as a genre is its namesake.

nodes.name: Music Institute
nodes.description: Detroit's short-lived, juice-bar-only techno club — the home floor of the first and second waves.

nodes.name: Second Summer of Love
nodes.description: Acid house hits Britain: warehouse parties, orbital raves, and a moral panic that forged UK dance culture.

nodes.name: Aretha Franklin
nodes.description: American singer whose recordings helped define soul music.
nodes.phaseNote: Editorial career prominence, approximately dated from her biography: gospel and Columbia beginnings, the 1967 Atlantic breakthrough, a mid-1980s crossover comeback, and later recordings. Shades are visual judgments, not measured popularity. The career ends with her last performances in 2017; posthumous listening is not modeled.

nodes.name: James Brown
nodes.description: American singer, bandleader and songwriter central to soul and funk.
nodes.phaseNote: Editorial career prominence anchored to the soul breakthrough, the mid-1960s and early-1970s funk records, and the 1985 Living in America crossover. These are approximate career eras, not chart or streaming scores. His active career ends in 2006.

nodes.name: Marvin Gaye
nodes.description: American soul singer and songwriter known for socially engaged and intimate recordings.
nodes.phaseNote: Editorial career prominence: early Motown success, the 1971 What's Going On period, later-1970s recordings, and the 1982 Sexual Healing comeback. Dates anchor a qualitative interpretation of his biography, not measured popularity; the active career ends in 1984.

nodes.name: Otis Redding
nodes.description: American soul singer and songwriter associated with Southern soul.
nodes.phaseNote: Editorial career prominence: early recordings followed by his mid-1960s Stax breakthrough. The career ends with his death in 1967; the posthumous success of (Sittin' On) The Dock of the Bay is not treated as another active-career phase.

nodes.name: Sam Cooke
nodes.description: American singer and songwriter whose work bridged gospel and soul.

nodes.name: Parliament-Funkadelic
nodes.description: American funk collective led by George Clinton.

nodes.name: Sly and the Family Stone
nodes.description: American band blending soul, funk and rock.

nodes.name: George Clinton
nodes.description: American singer, songwriter and producer who led Parliament-Funkadelic.

nodes.name: Prince
nodes.description: American singer, songwriter and multi-instrumentalist associated with Minneapolis funk.
nodes.phaseNote: Editorial career prominence: early solo releases, the 1980s breakthrough centered on Purple Rain, early-1990s success, and the 2004 Musicology comeback. Shades are qualitative and approximate, not measured popularity. The active career ends in 2016.

nodes.name: Donna Summer
nodes.description: American singer whose recordings became central to disco.
nodes.phaseNote: Editorial career prominence: musical-theatre beginnings, the 1975 breakthrough and late-1970s disco peak, the 1983 crossover, and later releases. The biography supports the milestones, not these numerical shades. The active career ends in 2012.

nodes.name: Chic
nodes.description: American disco and funk band founded by Nile Rodgers and Bernard Edwards.

nodes.name: Bee Gees
nodes.description: Pop group whose late-1970s recordings became closely associated with disco.
nodes.phaseNote: Editorial career prominence: late-1960s success, the Saturday Night Fever era, and later releases. The hidden stretches reflect the group's documented breaks after 2003, a 2006 performance, and the 2009 regrouping through 2012, not disappearance of interest in its catalogue. Shades are approximate, not popularity scores.

nodes.name: Sylvester
nodes.description: American singer associated with disco and Hi-NRG.

nodes.name: Grandmaster Flash and the Furious Five
nodes.description: Bronx hip-hop group known for DJ innovation and socially conscious lyrics.

nodes.name: Afrika Bambaataa
nodes.description: Bronx DJ and producer whose work connected hip-hop and electro.

nodes.name: Run-DMC
nodes.description: Queens hip-hop group that helped bring rap to a wider audience.

nodes.name: Public Enemy
nodes.description: American hip-hop group known for politically charged lyrics and dense production.

nodes.name: Can
nodes.description: German experimental rock group associated with the krautrock movement.

nodes.name: Neu!
nodes.description: German band whose motorik sound became influential in krautrock and later rock.
nodes.phaseNote: Editorial career phases: the original 1971–1975 recording period and the documented 1985–1986 reunion. The hidden gap represents inactivity of the band, not loss of influence. Relative shades within the active periods are qualitative.

nodes.name: Amon Düül II
nodes.description: German experimental rock group associated with krautrock.

nodes.name: Tangerine Dream
nodes.description: German electronic music group associated with the Berlin School and krautrock.

nodes.name: Faust
nodes.description: German experimental rock group associated with krautrock.

nodes.name: Gary Numan
nodes.description: English singer and songwriter whose early electronic pop helped shape synth-pop.
nodes.phaseNote: Editorial career prominence: Tubeway Army and the 1979 solo breakthrough, a quieter period, the darker sound from Sacrifice onward, and the later Savage and Intruder releases. Milestone dates are documented; these relative shades are not measured popularity.

nodes.name: Depeche Mode
nodes.description: English electronic music group that emerged from the early synth-pop scene.
nodes.phaseNote: Editorial career prominence anchored to early synth-pop, the late-1980s expansion, Violator and Songs of Faith and Devotion, then continuing releases including Memento Mori. The selected shades are not chart measurements and do not imply the band stopped between albums.

nodes.name: The Human League
nodes.description: English electronic pop group central to the development of synth-pop.
nodes.phaseNote: Editorial career prominence centered on Dare in 1981, Human in 1986, and the mid-1990s Tell Me When return. Later activity remains visible; the shades are an approximate interpretation of recording eras rather than a popularity series.
